n: Woe to Samaria, capital of Ephraim (northern Israel), sitting proudly on its hill above fertile valleys like a garland on the head of drunken partygoers. Its beauty is a fading flower.

f.g: Samaria, set on a hill like a wreath on a reveler’s head.

n: The Lord has a mighty one — Assyria — ready like a hailstorm, a destroying tempest, or a flood, to throw Samaria to the ground.

f.g: Assyria, which conquered Samaria in 722 BC.

n: Ephraim’s proud crown will be trampled underfoot.
Samaria’s fading glory will be like the first ripe fig of the season, snatched and eaten the moment someone sees it. Assyria will devour it just as eagerly.

f.g: The first-ripe fig, a prized early treat.

n: In that day the Lord Himself will be a glorious crown and beautiful diadem for the faithful remnant — a far better crown than Samaria’s.
He will give a spirit of justice to judges and strength to soldiers who drive enemies back at the gate.

f.w: turn the battle to the gate
f.g: Push attackers back to the city gate.

n: Now Isaiah turns to Judah: even its priests and prophets reel from wine and beer. They stagger when seeing visions and stumble when making judgments.
Their tables are covered with vomit; there is no clean place. A shocking image of spiritual and physical corruption.
The drunken leaders mock Isaiah: “Who does he think he’s teaching? Babies just weaned?” They resent being taught.
They mock his message as baby talk: “tsav la-tsav, kav la-kav” — sounds like a child’s singsong. Yet Latter-day Saints treasure the principle that God reveals truth line upon line.

f.g: In Hebrew, tsav la-tsav, tsav la-tsav, kav la-kav — possibly mocking nonsense syllables.

n: So be it, says Isaiah: God will speak to them with stammering lips and a foreign tongue — the Assyrian invaders. Paul applies this verse to speaking in tongues.
God had offered them rest and refreshment through trusting Him, but they would not listen.
So the word of the Lord will become to them just what they mocked — meaningless syllables — so that they stumble backward, are broken, trapped, and captured.
Listen, you scoffers who rule Jerusalem!
Judah’s leaders boasted that they had a “covenant with death” — likely a secret alliance with Egypt — and felt safe from the coming flood of Assyria. But they had hidden behind lies.

f.g: Possibly a jab at Egypt’s death-obsessed religion, or a treaty that only brings death.

n: God instead lays in Zion a tested, precious cornerstone, a sure foundation. Whoever trusts it will not panic. The New Testament and Book of Mormon identify this stone as Jesus Christ.

f.g: Will not flee in panic; Romans 9:33 reads “shall not be ashamed.”

n: God will use justice as His measuring line and righteousness as His plumb line. Hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and floods will wash out the hiding place.

f.g: Plumb line — a weighted cord used to check that walls are straight.

n: Their “covenant with death” will be canceled. When the overwhelming flood passes through, they will be beaten down by it.
Every time it passes it will catch them, morning after morning, day and night. Just understanding the message will bring terror.
A proverb: the bed is too short to stretch out on and the blanket too narrow to wrap up in. Their plans for safety won’t cover them.

The Lord will rise as He did at Mount Perazim and the valley of Gibeon, where He fought for David and Joshua. But now He will act against His own people — His “strange work.” Latter-day revelation also uses this phrase.
So stop mocking, or your chains will get tighter. Isaiah has heard from God that destruction is decreed for the whole land.
Isaiah now teaches with a farming parable: listen carefully to what I say.
Does a farmer plow forever? No — he plows and breaks up the soil only as long as needed.
Once the ground is leveled, he plants each seed in its proper place — dill, cumin, wheat in rows, barley, and spelt at the edges.

f.g: Black cumin or dill, a spice plant.

n: The farmer knows how to do this because God teaches him wisdom.
He doesn’t thresh delicate spices with a heavy sledge or cart wheel; he beats them gently with a stick.

f.g: A heavy sledge with sharp stones underneath.

n: Grain must be threshed to make bread, but not endlessly or so hard that it is crushed. Likewise, God’s judgments are measured — enough to refine, not to destroy.
This wisdom also comes from the Lord of hosts, whose counsel is wonderful and whose wisdom is great. He knows how much discipline each person needs.

f.g: Great in wisdom; abundant in success.
